records.place: Groppo, above Manarola in Riomaggiore, Cinque Terre DOC, Liguria

wine.name: Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà
wine.classification: DOC since 1973, created with the dry Cinque Terre white
wine.grapes: Bosco, the great majority by the co-operative's sheet, with a little Albarola and Vermentino; Bosco is the white grape that leads the Cinque Terre's blends.
wine.sites: Small terraced plots of the co-operative's members on the sea cliffs of the five villages, Riomaggiore, Manarola, Corniglia, Vernazza and Monterosso, on poor, stony ground held up by dry stone walls.
wine.making: Ripe bunches are picked by hand and laid on racks to dry naturally for about two months, by the co-operative's sheet. The must ferments on its skins and the wine is aged in small oak barrels; the DOC lets it go on sale only from 1 October of the year after the harvest, the Riserva not before the third year after it.
wine.glass: Amber with old gold glints; dried apricot, dried fig and acacia honey with a bitter orange edge; sweet and dense, lifted by fresh acidity, with a long finish of nuts and candied peel.
wine.ageing: Ready when it is released, it keeps for years in a cool cellar; the Riserva, aged at least three years in small oak by the house's sheet, is made to keep longer.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, poured in small measures beside blue cheese or almond biscuits.

label.means: The DOC's sweet wine of dried grapes, created in 1973 together with the dry Cinque Terre white.
A Sciacchetrà held back longer, released no earlier than the third year after the harvest.
The name under which the growers' co-operative of the five villages bottles its wines, at Groppo.

records.table: Cantina Cinque Terre, the growers' co-operative at Groppo above Manarola, makes its Sciacchetrà from Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino dried for weeks after picking. Amber and sweet, with dried apricot, fig and honey over a bitter orange edge, it wants a small glass and blue cheese.
records.story: Farmers have shaped the cliffs of the Cinque Terre over the past thousand years, as UNESCO describes the coast, cutting terraces for vines and holding them up with dry stone walls. In the twentieth century many of those terraces were abandoned. In 1973 the Cinque Terre DOC was created for the dry white and for Sciacchetrà, and in the same year a group of local growers founded a co-operative. Its legal name lists the villages whose growers it gathers, Riomaggiore, Manarola, Corniglia, Vernazza and Monterosso, and it bottles as Cantina Cinque Terre at Groppo above Manarola, in a cellar built in 1982 by the national park's account, taking grapes from many small plots so that the terraces stay farmed. In 1997 UNESCO inscribed Portovenere, the Cinque Terre and the islands of the gulf on its World Heritage List. The work is done by hand, with small monorail trolleys to carry the crates along the slopes. For a sommelier, the co-operative's Sciacchetrà is the way into the style: a sweet white of dried grapes from the sea cliffs, and one of the reasons the cliffs are farmed at all.

others.name: Cinque Terre
others.note: The co-operative's dry white of the same three grapes: lemon and a saline, herb scented finish, for anchovies and the fish of the coast.

others.name: Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà Riserva
others.note: The longer aged Sciacchetrà, at least three years in small oak, which the house describes with candied orange, dried figs, dried apricot and hazelnut.

others.name: Grappa Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà
others.note: Distilled by steam from the pomace of the co-operative's Sciacchetrà.

traps: Sciacchetrà is the Cinque Terre's sweet wine of dried grapes; Sciac-trà is the dry rosé of Ormeasco di Pornassio, from Dolcetto in the west of Liguria.
Sciacchetrà is not fortified: its sweetness and its strength come from grapes dried after picking, with no spirit added.
Cantina Cinque Terre is a co-operative of many growers across the five villages, not a single family estate.

cards.front: Which three grapes make the Sciacchetrà of Cantina Cinque Terre, and what is done to them before pressing?
cards.back: Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino, laid on racks to dry naturally for about two months.

cards.front: In what year was the Cinque Terre DOC created, and the growers' co-operative at Groppo founded?
cards.back: 1973, the year the DOC was created and a group of local growers began Cantina Cinque Terre.

questions.q: What makes the Sciacchetrà of Cantina Cinque Terre a sweet wine?
opts: Grapes dried for weeks after picking
Grape spirit added during fermentation
Grapes left to freeze on the vine
Sweet must added before bottling
questions.exp: Sciacchetrà is a passito: its grapes dry on racks for about two months before pressing, which concentrates their sugar; no spirit is added, so it is not a fortified wine.

questions.q: A group of local growers founded the co-operative that bottles as Cantina Cinque Terre in 1973. What else happened to the Cinque Terre's wine that year?
opts: Its DOC was created for the white and Sciacchetrà
Its terraces joined UNESCO's World Heritage List
Its national park was created by decree
Its first monorail was laid along the cliffs
questions.exp: The Cinque Terre DOC, for the dry white and Sciacchetrà, dates from 1973; UNESCO's inscription of the coast came later, in 1997.

report: Searches for this record: 9 of the group's 35, no fetch tried; the co-operative's own pages, read through search, give its legal name (Cooperativa Agricoltura di Riomaggiore, Manarola, Corniglia, Vernazza e Monterosso) and its label name, Cantina Cinque Terre, but no history page was found.

The founding of 1973 rests on Le Cinque Terre.org and a second account, read through search, of a co-operative begun by a group of local winemakers; the day of the DOC's decree, 29 May 1973, is given by the region record's source and by Ministry papers seen through Federvini and is left out for the cap of five sources.

The grapes' drying is in tension: Slow Food has them dried out of the sun for more than seventy days and a guide has shaded racks, while the national park's page has bunches dried in the sun until November; the record follows the first two and names Slow Food for the seventy days.

The disciplinare's release dates were amended in 2021 (from 1 November to 1 October, by the EU notice read through search), so the record gives a year after the harvest and the third year for the Riserva rather than a day; the share of Bosco (at least 40 per cent in one guide) was not read in the decree and is left out.

The 1982 date of the cellar's building at Groppo rests on one tour site and is left out; the name's origin in the Hebrew shekar is Slow Food's alone and is left out; the region record's small bottles were not confirmed and are not used.
The serving temperature follows the Codex's reference for sweet whites; the pairings are the region record's and a guide's (spiced cheeses, pandolce).
No living person is named; the co-operative's 220 members and its bottle counts are left out as volatile.
The group as a whole used 33 searches of its share of 35 (9, 8, 5, 4 and 7 by record), with no fetch tried.

changed: wine.grapes: "Bosco, the white grape that leads the Cinque Terre's blends, with Albarola and Vermentino."; now "Bosco, the great majority by the co-operative's sheet, with a little Albarola and Vermentino; Bosco is the white grape that leads the Cinque Terre's blends.": the co-operative's sheets give Bosco by far the larger part of both Sciacchetrà bottlings, with a little Albarola and Vermentino; the yearly figures are not printed.

wine.making: "Bunches dried for weeks out of direct sun and, by Slow Food's account, for more than seventy days, then destemmed by hand; the DOC lets it go on sale only a year after the harvest."; now "Ripe bunches are picked by hand and laid on racks to dry naturally for about two months, by the co-operative's sheet. The must ferments on its skins and the wine is aged in small oak barrels; the DOC lets it go on sale only from 1 October of the year after the harvest, the Riserva not before the third year after it.": the house's own sheets say the grapes dry naturally on racks for about two months, ferment with maceration on the skins and age in small oak, the Riserva at least three years; the hand destemming rested on Slow Food alone and is cut; the amended rules give 1 October of the year after the harvest and of the third year for the Riserva.

wine.ageing: "Ready when it is released, a year after the harvest, it goes on evolving for ten years and more; the Riserva, held back longer, keeps for longer."; now "Ready when it is released, it keeps for years in a cool cellar; the Riserva, aged at least three years in small oak by the house's sheet, is made to keep longer.": no source read gave a span of years; the Riserva's three years in small oak are the house's sheet.

story: "Vines have been the main crop of the Cinque Terre for at least a thousand years, by Slow Food's account ... many of those terraces were left to fall, as other work on the coast paid better than the vineyard."; now "Farmers have shaped the cliffs of the Cinque Terre over the past thousand years, as UNESCO describes the coast ... In the twentieth century many of those terraces were abandoned.": UNESCO's own description of the site speaks of the continuous history of settlement and the shaping of the terraced landscape over the past millennium; the reason for the abandonment rested on no source read.

story: "it bottles at Groppo above Manarola as Cantina Cinque Terre"; now "it bottles as Cantina Cinque Terre at Groppo above Manarola, in a cellar built in 1982 by the national park's account": the national park's page dates the cellar's building to 1982, and the author's tour site gave the same year; it adds a second dated turning point after the founding.

story: "on its World Heritage List, and programmes of repair since then have brought some abandoned terraces back to vines and olives."; now "on its World Heritage List.": the refuter read no source for the programmes of repair, so the clause is cut; the inscription of 1997 stands on UNESCO's page.

others[1].note and others[2]: "the Riserva without its oak; Cinque Terre Grappa, distilled from the marc of the co-operative's own Cinque Terre wines, Sciacchetrà among them"; now "the Riserva at least three years in small oak; Grappa Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà, distilled by steam from the pomace of the co-operative's Sciacchetrà": the house's shop names the grappa for the Sciacchetrà and gives its pomace and its steam distillation; the Riserva's oak is its own sheet.

cards[0].back and questions[0].exp: "dried for weeks out of direct sun, then destemmed by hand; dried for weeks before pressing"; now "laid on racks to dry naturally for about two months; its grapes dry on racks for about two months before pressing": to match the house's sheets, without the hand destemming.

sources: "the house's home page, Le Cinque Terre.org, Wineshop.it, the Slow Food presidium and UNESCO"; now "the house's two Sciacchetrà sheets, the Ministry's disciplinare page, the national park's page and UNESCO": the record now rests on the house's own sheets and the decree's own text; Slow Food's seventy days and thousand years are no longer told.
open: The drying: the house says naturally on racks for about two months, a producer's sheet racks out of the sun until November, and the national park's page by the author's report bunches dried in the sun; the record follows the house and makes no claim of sun or shade.
Bosco's least share in the Sciacchetrà was not read in the decree; the Cinque Terre white's 40 per cent in one guide is not carried over.

records.place: Arcagna, Dolceacqua, Rossese di Dolceacqua DOC, Riviera di Ponente, Liguria

wine.name: Bricco Arcagna
wine.appellation: Rossese di Dolceacqua or Dolceacqua DOC
wine.classification: DOC since 1972, the first of Liguria
wine.grapes: Rossese, the red grape of the hill country behind Ventimiglia and of the Dolceacqua valleys.
wine.sites: Vigna Arcagna, high on the Arcagna hill above Dolceacqua: steep terraces at around 400 metres on the flysch of Ventimiglia with clay, ground farmed since antiquity by the house's account.
wine.making: Picked by hand on the steep Arcagna terraces, destemmed and fermented in steel, the Rossese is then aged for about a year in oak barrels, barriques among them, before bottling. By the house's own account this makes Bricco Arcagna its richer reading of Rossese di Dolceacqua, set beside the bottling from the Terrabianca vineyard and its plain Rossese.
wine.glass: Pale to mid ruby; wild strawberry and bright red cherry, rose and black pepper, with Mediterranean scrub and a balsamic lift; light to medium in body, with fine, light tannin and a pleasing bitter edge.
wine.ageing: Fragrant within a few years of the vintage, while its perfume is bright; a strong year keeps for some years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, cool for a red; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass for its perfume, beside rabbit, the Ligurian way.

label.means: Two lawful names of one DOC, Liguria's first, for Rossese from the valleys behind Ventimiglia.
The crest of the Arcagna hill, bricco being a word of the north west for a hilltop.
White lands: the estate, named for the patch of white soil where the family planted its first Rossese.

records.table: Terre Bianche's Bricco Arcagna is Rossese di Dolceacqua from steep terraces high on the Arcagna hill above Dolceacqua, aged in oak barrels. Pale and perfumed, with wild strawberry, rose and black pepper, it should be poured cool, and rabbit is its Ligurian match.
records.story: Terre Bianche dates itself to 1870, when, by the family's account, an ancestor planted Rossese on a patch of white soil above Dolceacqua, the ground that gave the estate its name. The house traces the Arcagna hill much further back, to a small lookout tower of the ancient Ligurians, to the lands of a Roman family and to the estates of Benedictine monks, from the abbey of Novalesa by its account, who built a monastery of Santa Maria at Dolceacqua. When the Rossese di Dolceacqua DOC was decreed in 1972, the first in Liguria, the family was among the growers who founded it, as the house tells it. Over the following decades it gathered vines in small plots across the hills, made whites of Vermentino and Pigato beside its Rossese and opened its farmhouse to guests. Its Rossese comes from named vineyards, above all Terrabianca, the namesake on clay and blue marl, and Arcagna, on flysch; both are nomeranze, as Dolceacqua calls the named places that its DOC's rules allow on a label. Bricco Arcagna, from the crest of the hill and aged in oak, is the house's richer Rossese. For a sommelier it shows the far west of Liguria in a fuller key: a pale, perfumed red from one high hill, with the frame of time in wood.

others.name: Rossese di Dolceacqua Terrabianca
others.note: From the vineyard that named the estate, on clay and blue marl: the house's other named Rossese.

others.name: Rossese di Dolceacqua
others.note: The estate's plain Rossese, the way into the appellation before its two named vineyards.

others.name: Pigato
others.note: A white of the Riviera Ligure di Ponente, listed by the house beside its Vermentino.

traps: Rossese di Dolceacqua and Dolceacqua are two lawful names of one DOC, not two appellations.
Rossese di Dolceacqua, of 1972, was Liguria's first DOC; the Cinque Terre DOC followed in 1973.
Terre Bianche is the Dolceacqua estate; Terre Bianche Cuvée 161 is a Torbato of Sella & Mosca in Sardinia, an unrelated white.

cards.front: Which grape, which hill and which soil give Terre Bianche its Bricco Arcagna?
cards.back: Rossese, from the Arcagna hill above Dolceacqua, on flysch with clay at around 400 metres.

cards.front: Where does the Dolceacqua estate say its name, Terre Bianche, comes from?
cards.back: A patch of white soil where the family planted its first Rossese, in 1870 by its own account.

questions.q: Which appellation does Terre Bianche's Bricco Arcagna, a red of the far west of Liguria, carry on its label?
opts: Rossese di Dolceacqua
Riviera Ligure di Ponente
Ormeasco di Pornassio
Colli di Luni
questions.exp: Bricco Arcagna is Rossese di Dolceacqua, the DOC of the valleys behind Ventimiglia, which may also be written Dolceacqua; Riviera Ligure di Ponente is the broader DOC of the western coast.

questions.q: By the house's account, the family behind Terre Bianche was among the founders of the Rossese di Dolceacqua DOC, the first in Liguria. When was it decreed?
questions.exp: The DOC was decreed in 1972; 1870 is the year the house gives for its first Rossese, and the Cinque Terre DOC followed in 1973.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35, no fetch tried; the house's own pages, read through search, give 1870, the white soil, the Arcagna hill's history, the flysch with clay, the oak barrels and the family among the DOC's founders in 1972.

The plan's note is answered: 1870 is confirmed by Liguria Wine and other secondary accounts beside the house; labels and retailers print both Rossese di Dolceacqua and Dolceacqua, the DOC's two lawful names, and no source read calls Bricco Arcagna a Superiore, so the record claims neither.
Italy Traveller alone gives a late harvest, fermentation in steel and six months in barriques; the house says only oak barrels, so the record says aged in oak barrels and leaves the rest out.
The 380 to 450 metres and east facing slope of Vigna Arcagna, and Terrabianca's blue clay and marl at 360 to 380 metres, are the producer's own figures as quoted by retailers and read through search.
Arcagna and Terrabianca appear in the list of named places of the EU amendment of July 2025; one guide gives 2011 for the recognition of 33 such names, not confirmed, so no year is given.

The family member who planted in 1870 has no dates in any source and is described, not named; the agronomist of 1901 and his American rootstocks rest on the house alone and are left out; the farmhouse's opening year (1998 in one account) is left out.

Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Filippo Rondelli, who runs the estate and led the push to map its crus, Paolo Rondelli and Franco Laconi; Claudio Rondelli is reported dead in the late 1990s, without dates.
The region record calls Rossese the same vine as Provence's Tibouren as a fact, while one source read gives the identity with the direction of origin still debated; the record does not raise it.

changed: wine.sites: "steep terraces facing east at about 380 to 450 metres"; now "steep terraces at around 400 metres": AIS Lombardia gives 320 to 420 metres for Arcagna, the house's figures quoted by merchants 380 to 450; both hold around 400. The aspect was the house's alone as merchants quote it and is cut with the figure.

wine.making: "the Rossese is fermented and then aged in oak barrels before bottling"; now "destemmed and fermented in steel, the Rossese is then aged for about a year in oak barrels, barriques among them, before bottling": three listings and a review give about a year in oak, mostly barriques of 225 litres, after fermentation in steel; Vinopoly adds casks of 500 litres, so the record says barriques among them.

story: "to a lookout tower of the ancient Ligurians on Mount Aurin, to Roman landholders and to the estates of the Benedictine monks of Novalesa, who kept a monastery at Dolceacqua"; now "to a small lookout tower of the ancient Ligurians, to the lands of a Roman family and to the estates of Benedictine monks, from the abbey of Novalesa by its account, who built a monastery of Santa Maria at Dolceacqua": the house's page has the Aurinia, a Roman family, not a mountain, and the Benedictines' monastery of Santa Maria, Novalesa in its Italian version.

story: "farmed its Vermentino and Pigato organically"; now "made whites of Vermentino and Pigato beside its Rossese": the refuter read no source for organic farming; the whites stand on the house's list of wines.

story: "Terrabianca, the namesake on blue clay and marl, and Arcagna, higher on flysch, which the house calls by the old local word nomeranze"; now "Terrabianca, the namesake on clay and blue marl, and Arcagna, on flysch; both are nomeranze, as Dolceacqua calls the named places that its DOC's rules allow on a label": nomeranze is the local word for the DOC's additional geographical mentions, not the house's; the soils as the house and a merchant give them; Arcagna is not plainly higher once AIS's altitude is read.

others[0].note and others[2].note: "Terrabianca on blue clay and blue marl facing south east at about 360 to 380 metres; Pigato from vines the house farms organically"; now "Terrabianca on clay and blue marl, the house's other named Rossese; Pigato listed by the house beside its Vermentino": the aspect and altitude were the house's figures through merchants, untested; organic farming had no source the refuter read.

traps[1]: "the Cinque Terre followed in 1973, and Liguria has no DOCG"; now "the Cinque Terre DOC followed in 1973": Liguria's want of a DOCG is a present fact the refuter read in no source; the two dates stand on the decrees.
cards[0].back: "on flysch with clay at about 380 to 450 metres"; now "on flysch with clay at around 400 metres": as the sites.

sources: "Liguria Wine and Italy Traveller"; now "AIS Liguria (the first DOC of 1972) and Galli Enoteca (the barrels)": two independent sources for the first DOC, and a sheet for the making in place of the one account of a late harvest and six months in barrique.
open: Arcagna's altitude: 380 to 450 metres by the house as merchants quote it, 320 to 420 by AIS Lombardia; the record says around 400.
The year the nomeranze entered the rules, 2011 in Galli Enoteca and in a guide the author read, is left out for want of the decree's own text; the Ministry's text was modified twice in 2011.
The barrels of Bricco Arcagna: barriques of 225 litres in most accounts, casks of 500 litres beside them in one, used barriques in another; native yeasts in one sheet.

records.place: Castelnuovo Magra, Colli di Luni DOC, Riviera di Levante, Liguria

wine.name: Vermentino Etichetta Nera
wine.classification: DOC since 1989, shared by Liguria and Tuscany
wine.grapes: Vermentino, the white grape of the Ligurian coast; the DOC asks at least nine tenths of it for a wine named Vermentino.
wine.sites: Parcels in the hills of Luni and Castelnuovo Magra at the eastern end of Liguria, by the Tuscan border, chosen each year by the house for their aromatic promise.
wine.making: Picked by hand in the early morning and brought quickly to the cellar, the grapes are given a short cold maceration on their skins, then fermented at a controlled temperature in steel. The wine rests on its fine lees in steel for about four months before bottling, by the house's sheet.
wine.glass: Straw yellow; ripe apricot and yellow peach, acacia blossom and Mediterranean scrub, with a briny, balsamic note; full and rounded in body yet vivid with acidity and savoury, closing long on almond.
wine.ageing: Generous on release; drink it within a few years of the vintage, while its fruit is ripe and its saline edge fresh.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, beside fish, pesto or the anchovies of the coast.

label.means: The DOC of the hills around the old Roman port of Luni, decreed in 1989 and reaching into Tuscany.
Black label: the house's fuller Vermentino, first made with the 1992 vintage.
The house's name, after Luni, the ancient port of the coast below its hills.

records.table: Lunae Bosoni's Vermentino Etichetta Nera is the fuller Colli di Luni white of the house at Castelnuovo Magra: a short cold soak on its skins, then months on its lees in steel. Ripe with apricot, peach and Mediterranean scrub, it closes on almond; pour it with fish and pesto.
records.story: The Bosoni family farmed the Colli di Luni, the hills at the eastern end of Liguria where the coast turns towards Tuscany, and in 1966 one of its sons began making and selling wine of his own. He named the house Lunae, after Luni, the ancient port of the coast below, as the house tells it. His first wine from Vermentino, by the house's sheet, is the bottling it calls Etichetta Grigia, the grey label. In 1989 the hills became the Colli di Luni DOC, by a decree of 14 June that year, a denomination that runs from the province of La Spezia over the regional border into the north of Massa Carrara in Tuscany. Etichetta Nera followed with the 1992 vintage, after long research in the vineyard and the cellar, by the house's account: a Vermentino given a short time on its skins and months on its fine lees, for a fuller, rounder white than the coast's fresh, early bottled norm. The family went on to farm both the hill soils and the sandy plain of Luni, and to bottle the red Vermentino Nero beside its whites. For a sommelier, Etichetta Nera shows the riper side of Vermentino from the Colli di Luni: apricot and scrub, salt and almond, with weight enough for a main course of fish.

others.name: Vermentino Etichetta Grigia
others.note: The grey label, by the house's sheet the first wine its founder made from Vermentino.

others.name: Vermentino Nero
others.note: A red of the local Vermentino Nero grape, from foothill soils and the sandy plain of Luni, by the house's sheet.

traps: The Colli di Luni DOC crosses the regional border: part of it lies in Tuscany, in the province of Massa Carrara.
Etichetta Nera sees no oak: its fuller texture comes from a short maceration on the skins and months on the lees, all in steel.
Vermentino Nero, which the house also bottles, is a red grape and a red wine; Etichetta Nera is white Vermentino, and its black is the colour of the label.

cards.front: What gives the Etichetta Nera of Lunae its fuller texture without any oak?
cards.back: A short cold maceration on the skins, then some four months on its fine lees in steel.

cards.front: In which year was the house of Lunae Bosoni founded, and which vintage was the first Etichetta Nera?

questions.q: How does Lunae Bosoni make its Vermentino Etichetta Nera fuller than the coast's usual white?
opts: Brief skin contact, then months on the lees
A year of ageing in new French oak barrels
Grapes dried on racks for weeks before pressing
A second fermentation in the bottle, on yeast
questions.exp: The house gives Etichetta Nera a short cold maceration on the skins and about four months on its fine lees, all in steel; new oak would give vanilla and toast, which this wine does not have.

questions.q: In 1966 a son of the Bosoni family began the house of Lunae in the Colli di Luni. After what did he name it?
opts: Luni, the ancient port of the coast
A Roman villa found in his vineyard
A grape grown only in his hills
His first vineyard, bought that year
questions.exp: By the house's own account Lunae takes its name from Luni, the ancient port of the coast, which also names the Colli di Luni DOC of 1989.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, no fetch tried; the house's Etichetta Nera page and sheets, read through search, give the first vintage of 1992, the eight hours on the skins, the four months on fine lees in steel, the hand harvest and the hills of Luni and Castelnuovo Magra.

The plan's note is answered: the house writes its name Cantine Lunae, styled LVNAE, at Via Bozzi 63, Castelnuovo Magra; Lunae Bosoni, the plan's producer, is kept; its page names the wine Vermentino Etichetta Nera, Colli di Luni DOC, so the label term Colli di Luni Vermentino is not printed word for word.

The founding of 1966 rests on secondary accounts read through search (Quotidiano.net, Bottle of Italy and others), which agree on the year; one of them gives the founder as the fourth generation of a farming family, another his son as the fourth, so the story hedges the generation.

The DOC's decree of 14 June 1989 and the nine tenths of Vermentino are the AIS copy of the disciplinare, read through search; the house's sheet gives no soil for Etichetta Nera, so the sites carry none.

Pliny the Elder's praise of the wine of Luni rests on one regional source read and is left out; the house's claim that Luni was an Etruscan and Greek port is left out, and the Codex region record's Roman port is kept.
The ageing and serving lines are the author's, within the Codex's reference for full whites; the house's sheet read gives no serving temperature or keeping time.
Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Paolo Bosoni, the founder, and his son Diego Bosoni; the house keeps its name Lunae Bosoni.

changed: wine.making, table, story, traps[1], cards[0].back: "about eight hours of cold maceration on the skins; a few hours on its skins"; now "a short cold maceration on the skins; a short cold soak, a short time on its skins": the listings disagree on the skin contact, eight hours in most and up to forty eight in two, so the record says short and gives no figure; about four months on fine lees in steel stands on the house's sheet and the majority of listings.

wine.name: Chardonnay Cuvée Bois
wine.appellation: Valle d'Aosta or Vallée d'Aoste DOC
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, grown in the central valley.
wine.sites: Seven crus in several communes of the central valley, Aymavilles and Saint-Christophe among them, on terraced slopes at about 550 to 750 metres facing south, south east and north east; loose, sandy moraine over granite, with silt, limestone and much stone.
wine.making: Fermented in French oak barrels of 300 litres, half of them new and half in their second use, then aged in the same barrels on its lees for about a year, the lees stirred each week, by the house's sheet; the name Cuvée Bois speaks of the wood.
wine.glass: Straw yellow with golden glints; banana, candied citron and ripe white fruit over hazelnut, vanilla and acacia honey from the barrel; dense and rich in the mouth, with fresh acidity and a long, fine finish.
wine.ageing: Generous on release; its oak and lees give it the frame to develop in bottle over several years, gaining hazelnut and honey.
wine.serve: 12 to 13 degrees Celsius, the house itself pouring it up to 15; no need to decant; a wide, Burgundy style white wine glass.

label.means: The French form of the region's one DOC, equal to the Italian Valle d'Aosta on the label.
The grape named after the DOC, as the valley's rules allow for a wine of one variety.
Wood cuvée: the house's Chardonnay fermented and aged in oak barrels, beside its other Chardonnay.

records.table: Les Crêtes, at Aymavilles in the central Valle d'Aosta, makes its Chardonnay Cuvée Bois from seven crus on sandy moraine at up to about 750 metres, fermented in French oak and kept a year on its lees. Rich with hazelnut, vanilla and candied citron, it wants a wide glass.
records.story: The Charrère family came over the Alps around 1750 and settled at Aymavilles, on the sunny side of the central Valle d'Aosta, where it kept a house with old cellars and a water mill. By the region's account it pressed walnut oil and later cider and milled grain, until in 1955, as oil and flour came in from outside the valley, it turned to wine. In 1989 one of its members, who had left teaching for the vineyard, turned his wine business into a new estate, Les Crêtes, with vines on terraces in several communes of the central valley. The Valle d'Aosta is an Alpine valley with one DOC, written in Italian or French, and many of its grapes are found almost nowhere else; the estate became known for two of them, Petite Arvine and Fumin, and for Chardonnay. Chardonnay Cuvée Bois followed with the 1995 vintage, by the house's account: grapes from seven crus at about 550 to 750 metres on sandy moraine, fermented in French oak barrels and kept about a year on the lees, which are stirred each week. Its name says what sets it apart from the house's other Chardonnay: the wood. For a sommelier, Cuvée Bois shows the Valle d'Aosta beyond its native grapes: a mountain Chardonnay with the richness of oak and lees, kept fresh by the cool nights of the Alps.

others.name: Petite Arvine
others.note: The house's white of the native grape it shares with the Swiss Valais, fresh and saline.

others.name: Fumin
others.note: A red of the valley's darker, firmer native grape, peppery and structured.

traps: Cuvée Bois is Chardonnay, not a native grape: the valley's own whites are Prié Blanc and Petite Arvine.
Les Crêtes lies at Aymavilles in the central valley, not in the upper valley of Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle under Mont Blanc.
The Valle d'Aosta has one regional DOC, labelled in Italian or French; Cuvée Bois carries it with its grape named, not one of the seven sub-zones.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 35, no fetch tried; the house's Cuvée Bois page, read through search, gives the seven crus, the 550 to 750 metres and their aspects, the granitic moraine, the 300 litre French barrels half new, the twelve months on lees with weekly stirring, the first vintage of 1995 and its own serving advice of 13 to 15 degrees Celsius.

The plan's note is answered in part: 1989 is in the house's history and in the region's lovevda page; no source read calls Cuvée Bois the flagship in words, but Gambero Rosso's guide has singled it out in several vintages by the pages read, so the pick is kept and Petite Arvine stays in the others.

The family's coming from France around 1750 is in both the house and lovevda, which differ on the place (Grenoble in the house's page, today's Haute-Savoie in lovevda), so the record says France; the family member of 1750 has no dates and is not named.
The house's pages differ on the generations (five and six) and are not used; one secondary account gives first vines planted in 1955 and another 1810, both left out.
Saint-Christophe and Aymavilles as communes of the crus come from Vino.com, a retailer quoting the producer; one retailer gives ten months in oak, the house twelve, and the record says about a year.
The serving line follows the Codex's reference for full whites and gives the house's warmer figure beside it; the ageing line is the author's, since the house gives no keeping time for Cuvée Bois.
Living names met, none in the fragment, for people.json: Costantino Charrère, the founder of 1989, and the family members who run the estate with him.

By the region's account it pressed walnut oil and later cider and milled grain, until in 1955, as oil and flour came in from outside the valley, it turned to wine": Haute-Savoie, where the region's page has the family come from, was not French in 1750, and the house's Grenoble area is another place; the building's date is 1800 by the house and about 1750 by the region, so no date is given; the mill, the cider, the grain and 1955 are the region's page.

records.place: Morgex and La Salle, under Mont Blanc, upper Valle d'Aosta

wine.name: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
wine.appellation: Valle d'Aosta or Vallée d'Aoste DOC
wine.classification: A named sub-zone of the Valle d'Aosta DOC, under Mont Blanc
wine.grapes: Prié Blanc alone, a native white grape of the valley, grown on its own roots.
wine.sites: The members' small vineyards in the communes of Morgex and La Salle at the foot of Mont Blanc, from about 900 to 1,200 metres, on stony glacial soils, the vines trained on very low pergolas held up by posts of wood or stone.
wine.making: Prié Blanc ripens early and is picked before the snows, by the co-operative's account. Fermented in steel at a controlled temperature, the wine rests about eight months in steel and a month in bottle before it is released, by the house's sheet, which keeps the grape's light, fresh character.
wine.glass: Very pale; sage, wild flowers and citrus peel with a touch of exotic fruit; light in body, fresh and savoury, with a clean, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Made for drinking young, within a few years of the vintage, while it is crisp and fragrant.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, as an aperitif or beside trout.

label.means: The French form of the region's one DOC, equal to the Italian Valle d'Aosta; the sub-zone's name follows it.
The native white grape that the sub-zone allows alone, grown at Morgex and La Salle on its own roots.
The co-operative's name, which it also gives its still white of the sub-zone.

records.table: Cave Mont Blanc, the growers' co-operative of Morgex and La Salle, makes Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle from ungrafted Prié Blanc on low pergolas at up to about 1,200 metres. Pale and light, with sage, citrus peel and a saline edge, pour it cold as an aperitif.
records.story: At Morgex and La Salle, under Mont Blanc, Prié Blanc has long grown on very low pergolas close to the stony ground, which gives back by night the warmth it stores by day, and the dry mountain air keeps fungal disease rare, as the co-operative describes it. When phylloxera ravaged the vineyards of Europe at the end of the nineteenth century, the vines here were not grafted onto American roots, since at that height, as the valley tells it, the louse could do them no harm, and Prié Blanc has been grown on its own roots ever since. The growers' plots are small and steep: in 1971, at the urging of the parish priest of Morgex, they formed the Association des Viticulteurs, and in 1983, out of it, they founded a co-operative, the Cave du Vin Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, which later took the name Cave Mont Blanc de Morgex et La Salle. Beside the still white it makes sparkling wines by the traditional method, which by its own account it has made since 1983, among them a brut nature kept long on its lees. For a sommelier, the co-operative's still Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle is the plain statement of its sub-zone: light, fresh Prié Blanc from ungrafted vines, made in steel to keep the mountain in the glass.

others.name: Cuvée du Prince
others.note: A traditional method brut nature of Prié Blanc, first fermented in large larch and oak casks and in steel, then six years on its lees by the house's sheet.

others.name: Blanc du Blanc
others.note: A traditional method brut of Prié Blanc, pale with green glints, which the house describes with apple and wisteria.

traps: Prié Blanc is the only grape of Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle; Petite Arvine and Chardonnay are grown lower in the valley.
Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle is a named sub-zone of the Valle d'Aosta DOC, not a DOC of its own, and it is made still and sparkling.
Morgex and La Salle are communes of the upper Valle d'Aosta in Italy, not of Savoie or the Swiss Valais across the passes.

cards.front: How are the Prié Blanc vines of Cave Mont Blanc trained, and on what roots?
cards.back: On very low pergolas held up by posts of wood or stone, on their own roots, never grafted.

cards.front: Under what name was the co-operative of Morgex and La Salle founded in 1983?
cards.back: Cave du Vin Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle; it later took the name Cave Mont Blanc.

questions.q: Why can Cave Mont Blanc grow the Prié Blanc for its Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle on its own roots?
opts: Phylloxera does the vines no harm at that height
The vineyards lie on pure, loose sand
The vines are flooded every winter
The vines are replanted every few years
questions.exp: At about 900 to 1,200 metres phylloxera could not harm the vines, so Prié Blanc was never grafted; sand protects ungrafted vines in places such as Colares, not under Mont Blanc.

questions.q: In which year did the growers of Morgex and La Salle found the co-operative that became Cave Mont Blanc?
questions.exp: The co-operative was founded in 1983 as the Cave du Vin Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, out of an earlier growers' association; 1989 is the year Les Crêtes was founded lower in the valley.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35, no fetch tried; the co-operative's pages, read through search, give the low pergolas on posts of wood or stone, the early harvest before the snows, the still wine's sheet (Prié Blanc on its own roots at 900 to 1,200 metres, eight months in steel and one in bottle, 8 to 10 degrees Celsius) and the Cuvée du Prince sheet (brut nature, 72 months on lees).

The plan's note is answered: the bottling taught is the still DOC white, which the house lists under its own name among its whites; Rayon appears only in a list of aroma notes and no sheet of it was found, so it is not used. The house writes its name Cave Mont Blanc de Morgex et La Salle, Società Cooperativa.

The founding of 1983 under the name Cave du Vin Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle rests on the Chamber of Commerce's record and on the region's lovevda listings, which keep the old name in their address; the move into its buildings in 1989 is the Chamber's alone and is told as its record; no year was found for the change of name.

The house's page dates the traditional method in its cellar to 1983, and calls itself the only house of the valley making DOC sparkling wine by that method; the record keeps the date as the house's and makes no claim of a first or an only.

Left out for want of a second source: an earlier growers' association and a parish priest of Morgex credited with uniting the growers, the first bottles three years after the founding, the mention of the wine in a document of 1291, and the year the DOC took in the sub-zone, which no source read gave.

Chaudelune, the house's wine from grapes left to freeze, is left out of the others: no sheet of it was read. The members' number and the bottles a year differ between sources and are volatile, so none is given.
The ageing line is the author's, for a white aged eight months in steel; the house gives no keeping time. No living person is named.
